abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a critical nosocomial pathogen responsible for severe and often difficult-to-treat infections in humans. Despite their central role in early host-pathogen interactions, the carbohydrate-binding lectins LecA and LecB remain largely underexplored compared to other P. aeruginosa virulence factors. Here, we show that LecA and LecB activate the human receptor tyrosine kinase EphA2 in a time- and carbohydrate-dependent manner in lung epithelial cells. Whereas LecB directly engages EphA2 primarily through protein-glycan binding, LecA activates EphA2 indirectly via interactions with the glycosphingolipid Gb3. Both lectins strongly colocalize with EphA2 at the host plasma membrane and trigger downstream CrkII phosphorylation via canonical EphA2 signaling. Owing to their tetravalent nature, LecA and LecB can cross-link membrane receptors, driving lateral membrane reorganization that initiates downstream signaling. Moreover, simultaneous engagement of both lectins at the plasma membrane further potentiates EphA2 activation. Finally, we demonstrate that live P. aeruginosa preferentially adheres to membrane domains where EphA2 concomitantly accumulates, inducing receptor activation in host cells. Collectively, these findings identify EphA2 as a pivotal host receptor mediating LecA- and LecB-driven signal transduction and provide new mechanistic insights into how P. aeruginosa exploits human lung epithelial cells during infection.
